[parlaylib](https://github.com/cmuparlay/parlaylib) is a C++ library for parallel programming with its own custom work-stealing scheduler that makes it faster than alternatives (e.g. OpenMP or Cilk) for irregular workloads.
Here, I solve the 8th exercise from the 2025 Advent of Code. TODO: link to the problem

## Work Stealing

The general challenge that ParlayLib must solve is to assign threads (maximal sequences of instructions without synchronization) to system processes that can execute them.
In the fork-join model (in which we have a *pardo(f1, f2)* primitive that executes *f1* and *f2* in concurrently, joining so that the next instruction is executed only after both are completed.
The work $W$ of an algorithm is the total number of instructions, and the span $S$ is the longest sequence of dependent instructions.

In the offline setting, in which the scheduler can see the entire task dependency graph, the greedy scheduler is a 2-approximation of optimality.
For $P$ processors, the greedy scheduler completes in at most $W/P + S$ time.

In the online setting, the overhead of an idle processor taking a task is nontrivial.
Thus, it makes sense to introduce process-local queues.
Work stealing is this paradigm: have local dequeues, taking work from the bottom of its work deque, and if empty, then stealing from the top of another processors.
Stealing randomly (choosing a processor at random and popping from the top) is near-optimal (TODO: attach proof).

## ParlayLib

In addition to the scheduler, perhaps the nicest part about using parlay is its comprehensive set of examples and work-efficient library functions.
We can do prefix sums, filters, maps, etc. in linear work and logarithmic span.
It also provides nice atomic primitives, such as `write_min` that uses the compare-and-swap to atomically update the minimum value.

# The Puzzle

Here, I focus on part 2 of the day 8 puzzle.
As input, we have $N = 1000$ points in 3D space (integer coordinates).
We must simulate Kruskals algorithm for building an MST, and find the last edge added.
For all inputs, this last edge will is unique.

## Sequential Kruskals

Of course, the simple approach is to just implement it.
For all $\binom{N}{2}$ pairs of node, we append an edge connecting them, with weight the squared distance (so that we use integer operations, rather than floating point and sqrts).
Sort all edges, merge them sequentially using a Union Find implementation, and record the last edge added.

We get a time of about 75ms (using `hyperfine` as the benchmark runner)

```console
Benchmark 1: ./build/main kruskal_seq < data.in
  Time (mean ± σ):      75.5 ms ±   3.3 ms    [User: 68.9 ms, System: 6.1 ms]
  Range (min … max):    70.1 ms …  85.7 ms    39 runs
```

Seeing where the time is at, we can use `perf`.

```console
+   98.81%     0.00%  main     main                  [.] _start
+   98.81%     0.00%  main     libc.so.6             [.] __libc_start_main@@GLIBC_2.34
+   98.81%     0.00%  main     libc.so.6             [.] __libc_start_call_main
+   98.81%     0.00%  main     main                  [.] main
+   98.77%    15.16%  main     main                  [.] solve_kruskal_seq(std::vector<Point3D, std::alloc
+   84.58%    84.55%  main     main                  [.] void std::__introsort_loop<__gnu_cxx::__normal_it
     0.08%     0.01%  main     ld-linux-x86-64.so.2  [.] _dl_lookup_symbol_x
...
```

As expected, nearly 85% of the the time is in the `std::sort` of the 500k edges.
Remembering that our edges are integers, a simple radix sort makes this much better.

```console
Benchmark 2: ./build/main kruskal_seq_parlay < data.in
  Time (mean ± σ):      25.9 ms ±   2.2 ms    [User: 16.9 ms, System: 10.3 ms]
  Range (min … max):    20.2 ms …  31.0 ms    98 runs
```

## Parallelizing Kruskals

We can do much better: 25 milliseconds is much too slow.
First, let's parallelize this.

Using a parallel radix sort over the edges, we get to about 20ms (TODO: show).
To do better with Kruskals, we would have to look at fewer edges.

Let's use quicksort: we partition the edges by weight, find the minimum spanning forest only using the light edges, and then prune the heavy edge set.
Any edge in the heavy set that is between two nodes that are already connected can be pruned.
This is known as filter-kruskals (TODO: cite), and is a bit faster.

```console
Benchmark 3: ./build/main kruskal_par < data.in
  Time (mean ± σ):      18.8 ms ±   1.6 ms    [User: 52.4 ms, System: 57.7 ms]
  Range (min … max):    15.5 ms …  24.7 ms    132 runs
```

We can even push this further, and note that we don't actually need the MST, but only the bottleneck MST.
Essentially, it is the same procedure: binary search on the edge weight, essentially what quicksort is.
To check if the bottleneck edge weight is lower or higher than our pivot, we can check if the lower is connected.

## Boruvkas

Another simple parallelizable algorithm for computing minimum spanning trees is known as Boruvkas.
At each step, we identifty at least $n / 2$ edges that can be added into the MST, where $n$ is the number of components we have (initially $N$ ).
The work recurrence follows $T(n) = O(n^2) + T(n/2)$, and costs quaderatic work.
We obtain $S(n) = O( \log n ) + S(n/2)$, and $O(\log^2(n))$ span.

The elegant part is that identifying these edges is super parallel: each node just finds the shortest boundary edge (in another component) in its neighborhood.
Indeed, looking at the results, we do beat parallel kruskals.
In fact, the work that we do is genuinely smaller (asymptotically), as we do less passes over the edgelist.

We can see that our input points are all quite regular in the 3D cube, and so the edge weights in the MST are all quite similar (TODO).
This could lead to the filtering heuristic not being as good as reported in the paper, though it is just a hypothesis.

### Removing the Edgelist

Each of our improvements above seem to have diminishing returns.
Examining our `perf` a little more, we can see why: maintaining a sequence of 500k edges is just expensive.

For each component in our MST, we must find the shortest boundary edge (i.e. to another component).
If our component is of size $k$, then there is $k \times N$ edges incident to the component that we check.
This is different from the standard Boruvkas, where after each round, we deduplicate the edgelist so that there are no intra-component edges and no parallel edges between components.
A highly parallel write min loop later, and we get our fastest result by far:

TODO: why the reduce_by_index is not good here.

```cpp
auto best = parlay::tabulate<std::atomic<Distance>>(
  points.size(),
  [](size_t) { return Distance::Infty(); }
);

parlay::parallel_for(
  0, points.size(), [&](size_t u) {             // for each node u
  for (size_t v = 0; v < points.size(); ++v) {  // and neighboring node v
   if (labels[u] != labels[v])                  // in different components
    parlay::write_min(                          // update min dist
      &out[labels[u]],                          // for the component of u
      points[u].SqDistance(points[v]            // to include edge uv
    ));  
  }
);
```

# Conclusions

There are lots of ideas to make this better.
With data driven design (link to the cppcon talk), the struct of arrays pattern may make distance calculations more ammenable for vectorization.

Not mentioned, but the representation of Distance as trivially copyable as a uint64 was very important in making the edgelist fit in cache (TODO: check sizes)
and potentially a factor towards which the Boruvkas is so fast.

Perhaps the biggest way of saving time is to get better heuristics for partitioning the edgelist.
I mentioned earlier that our points seem to fit pretty regularly into a cube.
There are poeople TODO who take advantage of this!
Optimizing an algorithm for a particular family of instances is also important.

As a final note, for Euclidean minimum spanning trees, our $O(n^2)$ work is not optimal.
In 3D space, $O(n^{4/3})$ work is achievable (TODO: cite), though the details are too in the weeds for me to understand as of now.

Whooh.
This has been fun.
The extensive primitives parlay provides allows us to write, in a very concise manner, complex algorithms that perform effectively.
It is also a reminder to always measure the performance of code and instrument it: there are always an infinitude number of ways to improve one's code.
